title: Fixed-Price Guaranteed Clearance of Unknown Lead Lines
one_liner: Take the whole unknown-lines problem at a fixed price per line with an acceptance guarantee, and make money by routing each line to the cheapest method that will satisfy the state (records mining, meter-swap photos, paid photos, probe, pothole).
customer: Utilities with 5,000-100,000 unknown lines and a deadline, and the state programs or state revolving fund offices that want a known cost to fund. Wedge: a mid-size utility that has run out of staff or budget for engineering time-and-materials billing and can issue phased task orders under the small-purchase limit ($25-50k each). Later customer: a state that buys 'unknown clearance' for all its small systems.
problem: The industry sells effort: engineering firms bill hours, probe vendors sell hardware or crew days, modelers sell licenses, and portals sell software seats. No one sells the outcome the utility actually needs, which is 'this unknown line is now known and the state accepted it.' Utilities carry the acceptance risk, the routing decision and the cost overrun. The cost ladder is steep and poorly used: a records lookup can cost a few dollars, a photo $6-40, a scheduled visit around $120, a probe crew several hundred, a pothole about $900 or more, and a replacement thousands. Most utilities either dig too much or wait years.
solution: An 'unknowns clearing' contractor with a router at its core. Tier 0: predictive scores and assessor data on year built and neighborhood (bought from BlueConduit, VODA or open sources). Tier 1: vision-model mining of the utility's own tap cards, plumbing permits and old work orders, handwritten records that are now readable by multimodal models at $1-3 per line. Tier 2: three-photo protocol captured during meter swaps, inspections, water-heater changes and owner self-ID through a leadCAST- or Esri-style intake. Tier 3: scheduled visit by a panel plumber. Tier 4: probe or acoustic crew subcontracted from Electro Scan- or Echologics-type providers. Tier 5: pothole. Each line goes to the cheapest tier that the state accepts for that housing and meter archetype. The company quotes a blended fixed price per unknown (about $60-70) for a portfolio, guarantees acceptance (a rejected reclassification is redone free and the fee refunded), and holds a reserve for rejections. Evidence is exported in the state format and feeds the utility's Esri layer. First product for a scrappy team: an 800-1,000-line pilot with a spreadsheet-and-vision-model router and part-time inspectors.
why_now: Multimodal models can read old tap cards and permits and classify pipe photos, which collapses the cost of tiers 1 and 2 in 2025-2026. Inventory rules and the replacement clock (federal details still in flux, several state statutes independent of them, verify) make 'unknown' a budget line. Infrastructure-law SRF money is under spend-down pressure and funders prefer priced outcomes. Utilities are short of engineers, so buying an outcome is more attractive than buying hours. The photo, probe and prediction vendors now exist as suppliers to a router, which they did not five years ago.
revenue_model: Fixed price of about $60-70 per unknown, contracted in phased task orders of 500-1,000 lines each. Target blended cost is $28-35 per line, a rejection reserve of about 8%, and gross margin of roughly 45-50% at scale. Working capital comes from an initial reserve of a few hundred thousand dollars, then from SRF draws on accepted lines, and eventually acceptance-risk reinsurance so a third party underwrites the guarantee. Upside comes from the router's data: measured accuracy and cost per method by housing archetype, which improves margin every contract and can be sold to states as a benchmark. Later, sell state-wide 'unknown clearance' bundles.
non_obvious_insight: There are two inversions. First, price the outcome, not the effort. Hourly engineering firms and hardware vendors cannot copy a fixed price per accepted line without cannibalizing their own revenue. Second, treat the competitors as suppliers. Every tier below the pothole is somebody else's product, and the profit is in the routing decision and the guarantee, not in owning a method. The bigger unlock is that most unknowns turn out to be non-lead, so the cheapest method that proves it is almost always far below the dig cost. That spread, multiplied across tens of millions of unknowns nationally (verify with public inventory totals), is the business.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: pick one state with a written acceptance path. Approach five utilities in it and ask for a sample of their tap cards and unknown list. Run the vision model on 200 cards and measure how many lines it resolves. Days 10-20: build the router as a spreadsheet: for each address, cost, expected accept rate and method by tier. Line up one probe subcontractor and 10 part-time inspectors. Days 20-30: quote the first utility a fixed $65 per line for 800 unknowns, with a rejection reserve of $40k and a right to redo any rejected line free, structured as two task orders under the small-purchase limit. Ask the state program to confirm the acceptance path in writing before signing.
lineage: mutation of I0463 ('Pay Home Inspectors to Find Lead Pipes'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: BlueConduit, VODA.ai (Lead Finder / Lead Zero / Lead Management Dashboard), Trinnex leadCAST (used by Durham, NC), Esri ArcGIS Lead Service Line Inventory solution. White space: Nobody I found runs the specific thing proposed: a paid supply-side network of trade professionals (inspectors, plumbers, water-heater installers) who photograph the service entry under a fixed protocol, with vision-AI classification, tamper-evident geo-verification, human QA, and export to state inventory formats, sold to utilities per verified line. Players fall into four groups. (1) Predictive modelers (BlueConduit, VODA.ai) reduce digs statistically but still need ground-truth field samples, and Texas does not accept predictive modeling for official inventories. (2) Customer self-ID portals (Trinnex leadCAST, Esri Survey123, Cognito Forms) collect photos and reach only the 10-25% of owners who respond, and absentee landlords and LLCs almost never do. (3) Hardware probes (Electro Scan, Echologics) need a utility crew at each line. (4) Door-to-door inspection programs (RCAP, engineering firms) are staffed centrally and slowly. The unserved wedge is professional-grade evidence for the non-responding, owner-absent lines at about $30-60 per line, collected by people already inside the building. Two sub-gaps stand out: states that reject modeling but accept documented visual verification, and small or mid-size utilities with no field crews. Caveats: (a) my WebSearch budget ran out after 4 searches, so Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt and GitHub sweeps were not done and a stealth or very early startup in this niche could exist; (b) the search snippet says physical identification methods 'must be conducted or overseen by water system personnel' (state-dependent), so third-party photos may only count as self-ID-grade evidence unless the utility or state accepts contractor verification; (c) the idea's own note that regulatory details are from memory still applies; (d) per-utility supply is limited to home sales and water-heater swaps, so density per utility could be slow; (e) inspectors may resist liability for calling a pipe lead (my recollection, unverified); (f) Trinnex or Esri could add a 'contractor submission' role cheaply. | How this version avoids them: BlueConduit and VODA.ai sell predictions and licenses without taking verification or acceptance risk, and here they are tier-0 suppliers. Trinnex leadCAST, Esri Survey123 and DIY forms become the free intake layer for owners who respond. Electro Scan and Echologics/Mueller are hardware vendors that become tier-4 subcontractors rather than substitutes. RCAP door-to-door inspections are a potential tier-3 subcontractor. Stantec and other engineering firms bill time and materials and would have to give up their margin model to match a fixed price with a guarantee, which is counter-positioning. The parent's single-method network becomes one tier among six, and the company is not exposed to one regulator ruling on third-party photos.

competitors.name: BlueConduit
competitors.what_they_do: Category leader in machine-learning prediction of lead service line material. Products include LSL Predictions and LSL Unknown Management (representative field investigations, statistical classification of unknowns, auto-formatted state inventory templates). They claim 2-3 months to classify unknowns vs 3-10+ years by physical verification, and over $4.5M saved for a system with 5,000 unknowns. Does not appear to run a photo, contractor or crowdsourced verification network. It competes for the same 'shrink the unknowns' budget by reducing how many lines need any field check.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Over 1M lines inventoried, 50+ US/Canadian cities (Detroit, South Bend, Flint), NSF partnership, Sourcewell contract vehicle; Bloomberg Law says Detroit avoided about $380M of excavation. Funding amount not confirmed (search budget ran out).

competitors.name: VODA.ai (Lead Finder / Lead Zero / Lead Management Dashboard)
competitors.what_they_do: ML prediction of public and private lead laterals, sampling and replacement targeting, and a dashboard tracking inventory and replacement goals for LCRR/LCRI compliance. Their page shows no photo, self-ID or contractor verification features.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Funding and customer count not verified.

competitors.name: Trinnex leadCAST (used by Durham, NC)
competitors.what_they_do: Lead service line management portal. Durham residents upload photos of where the pipe enters the building and get a $30 water-bill credit once the utility approves the verification. Utility staff review submissions, and city-authorized inspectors do right-of-entry visits. It already covers customer-photo intake, incentive payment and utility review. It has no vision AI or trade-professional bounty network that I could confirm.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Vendor size and funding not found. Product family is assetCAST, leadCAST, waterCAST and dataCAST.

competitors.name: Esri ArcGIS Lead Service Line Inventory solution
competitors.what_they_do: Free template inside the GIS most utilities already own. It includes a public 'Water Service Line Material Survey' where residents submit material plus a photo, and an ArcGIS Field Maps app where crews record 'Utility Side Verified' and 'Customer Side Verified'. Any utility can stand up basic photo intake and field capture at near-zero software cost.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Incumbent GIS platform bundled with existing Esri utility licenses. No incremental funding needed.

competitors.name: Electro Scan Inc. (Swordfish probe, Critical H2O cloud app)
competitors.what_they_do: Insertion probe that measures electrical resistance to identify copper, galvanized, lead or plastic service lines without excavation. Results upload to a cloud app and GIS. Rock Hill, SC bought two full units and focused on about 14,000 pre-1989 homes; the EPA has done verification calls on its results.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Per-line pricing not disclosed. Rock Hill purchased two complete units.

competitors.name: Echologics / Mueller Water Products PipeScreen Service Line Analyzer
competitors.what_they_do: Acoustic two-sensor tool that detects lead service lines in minutes without entering the home or excavating. It is sold by a large public water-products incumbent that could bundle verification services.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Sold by Mueller Water Products (public company). Pricing not disclosed.

competitors.name: RCAP / Great Lakes Community Action Partnership in-home inspection service
competitors.what_they_do: Non-profit technical assistance that does door-to-door in-home inspections to verify customer-side service line material for rural systems, described as 'cost-effective' with minimal equipment. It is the human-visual-inspection model this idea proposes, but centrally staffed and not a marketplace or AI product.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Grant-funded non-profit network. No pricing published.

competitors.name: Stantec and other engineering firms (machine learning plus field verification programs)
competitors.what_they_do: Engineering consultancies bundle predictive modeling (Stantec partners with BlueConduit) with field verification crews for utilities. They are the usual channel for utility inventory work and will likely subcontract or compete with any verification vendor.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Large public engineering firm. Page text could not be fetched, so details are from the search snippet only.

competitors.name: DIY self-ID forms (Chesterfield County VA on Cognito Forms; Massachusetts DEP crowdsourcing application)
competitors.what_they_do: Utilities and states run free web forms where customers submit pipe material with photos, with a signed affidavit in some states. This is the zero-cost substitute the product must beat on accuracy and response rate. Chesterfield offers no incentive and relies on voluntary participation.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Free or cheap. Built on commodity form tools and Smartsheet.

I0463.white_space: Nobody I found runs the specific thing proposed: a paid supply-side network of trade professionals (inspectors, plumbers, water-heater installers) who photograph the service entry under a fixed protocol, with vision-AI classification, tamper-evident geo-verification, human QA, and export to state inventory formats, sold to utilities per verified line. Players fall into four groups. (1) Predictive modelers (BlueConduit, VODA.ai) reduce digs statistically but still need ground-truth field samples, and Texas does not accept predictive modeling for official inventories. (2) Customer self-ID portals (Trinnex leadCAST, Esri Survey123, Cognito Forms) collect photos and reach only the 10-25% of owners who respond, and absentee landlords and LLCs almost never do. (3) Hardware probes (Electro Scan, Echologics) need a utility crew at each line. (4) Door-to-door inspection programs (RCAP, engineering firms) are staffed centrally and slowly. The unserved wedge is professional-grade evidence for the non-responding, owner-absent lines at about $30-60 per line, collected by people already inside the building. Two sub-gaps stand out: states that reject modeling but accept documented visual verification, and small or mid-size utilities with no field crews. Caveats: (a) my WebSearch budget ran out after 4 searches, so Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt and GitHub sweeps were not done and a stealth or very early startup in this niche could exist; (b) the search snippet says physical identification methods 'must be conducted or overseen by water system personnel' (state-dependent), so third-party photos may only count as self-ID-grade evidence unless the utility or state accepts contractor verification; (c) the idea's own note that regulatory details are from memory still applies; (d) per-utility supply is limited to home sales and water-heater swaps, so density per utility could be slow; (e) inspectors may resist liability for calling a pipe lead (my recollection, unverified); (f) Trinnex or Esri could add a 'contractor submission' role cheaply.
I0463.evidence_of_demand: Moderate to strong for the problem, and only indirect for this specific mechanism. (1) Utilities already pay households to submit pipe photos. Durham offers a $30 water-bill credit for a verified self-ID with photos, which validates the incentive price point and the photo-as-evidence approach (https://www.durhamnc.gov/5184/Water-Service-Line-Inventory-and-Verific). The same page tells residents to check their home-inspection report because 'the home inspector may have identified your service line material and included a photo', so inspector photos are already used ad hoc but nobody pays for them. (2) Verification cost and time pain are quantified by a vendor: BlueConduit claims physical verification takes 3-10+ years and that a system with 5,000 unknowns can save over $4.5M and 5 years, which implies roughly $900 per unknown by digging (https://blueconduit.com/lsl-unknown-management/). (3) Utilities buy verification technology. Rock Hill, SC purchased two Swordfish units and targeted about 14,000 homes (https://trenchlesstechnology.com/identifying-water-service-line-pipe-materials-using-machine-intelligent-technology/), and Detroit's use of BlueConduit avoided an estimated $380M of excavation (https://news.bloomberglaw.com/environment-and-energy/ai-speeds-cities-lead-pipe-search-with-epa-deadline-weeks-away). (4) Regulatory pressure and the modeling gap: the EPA's October 2024 LCRI requires identifying and replacing lead pipes within 10 years (https://www.epa.gov/ground-water-and-drinking-water/lead-and-copper-rule-improvements). Bloomberg Law reports many systems filed substantial 'unknown' counts, the NRDC calls it a fundamental problem, and Texas does not accept predictive modeling for official inventories, which forces physical or visual verification. (5) Funding tie-in: BIL provides $15B for LSL replacement through state revolving funds, and BlueConduit notes systems win funding most often when they minimize unknowns first (https://blueconduit.com/post/what-funding-is-available-for-replacing-privately-owned-lead-service-lines/). Not found: any RFP, forum thread or purchase order for per-line paid third-party photo verification, or any home inspector asking to be paid for this. That demand is unproven.
I0463.sharper_angle: Do not lead with a consumer-facing inspector bounty marketplace, where free Esri and Survey123 forms and leadCAST-style portals with a $30 credit already cover the customer-photo layer. Position as the verification-grade evidence and field-sampling layer that plugs into the tools utilities and consultants already use. Three moves. (1) Sell to the predictive modelers and engineering firms first (BlueConduit, VODA.ai, Stantec, Hazen-type consultants). Their models require 'representative field investigations' and ground-truth samples, and states like Texas require physical verification. Offer a per-line, tamper-evident, professionally collected photo sample at a fraction of potholing cost, so you are the channel partner rather than a competitor with a 6-12 month municipal sales cycle. (2) Replace recruit-and-pay-each-inspector with distribution through chokepoints that already put a trade professional next to the pipe. That means embedding the 3-photo protocol as a module in home-inspection report software, and as a water-heater or plumbing-permit closeout requirement that utilities or cities can mandate for near-zero bounty. Target absentee-landlord and LLC-owned rentals through rental registration and inspection programs, the cohort self-ID portals cannot reach. (3) Start in one state that explicitly accepts documented contractor or visual verification and rejects pure modeling. Get a written acceptance letter from the state drinking-water program before selling anything, and publish potholed ground-truth accuracy on the first 200 lines. Integrate outputs into Esri and leadCAST rather than replacing them. Before building, confirm with 3-5 state programs whether third-party photo verification can reclassify an 'unknown' line to non-lead or lead, and with 10 inspectors whether they will accept the liability and effort for $15-25 per line.
